claims.text: The proposed CoCrFeNi-based multilayer coating contains distinct interfaces formed by thin carbon or graphene layers within the HEA matrix.
The carbon- or graphene-containing interfaces are coherent.
Coherent multilayer interfaces act as robust barriers to dislocation motion.
The interfaces hinder both dislocation climb and dislocation glide.
Hindering dislocation motion increases the effective activation energy for creep.
Increasing the effective activation energy for creep limits the accumulation of plastic strain over time.
A multilayer coating containing an engineered interfacial phase can be compared with a homogeneous single-phase HEA film lacking those interfaces.
An inert testing atmosphere minimizes oxidation during elevated-temperature creep or nanoindentation testing.
The coherent interfacial barriers promote dislocation pile-up and impede dislocation transmission across layers.
Elevated-temperature creep in a CoCrFeNi-based HEA can be mediated by dislocation climb.
During sustained loading, interface-induced dislocation pile-ups redistribute stress in the multilayer coating.
The multilayer coating will have a lower creep rate and accumulate less plastic strain than the homogeneous HEA coating.
Post-test microscopy will reveal dislocation pile-ups at the multilayer interfaces.
The proposed interface-controlled mechanism applies in temperature and stress regimes dominated by dislocation-mediated creep.
The mechanism may not apply when diffusion creep prevails, typically at higher temperatures or lower stresses.
The quantitative effects of interface strength, spacing, and chemistry on deformation remain uncertain.
Failure to observe either a statistically significant creep-rate reduction or interfacial dislocation pile-up would falsify the proposed interface mechanism.
